speakers: Dave Drew (systematic trader, former apprentice of Ed Seykota)
summary: Bonus part of an Open Interest interview: Dave Drew recounts six months as Ed Seykota's apprentice and what he learned. Seykota was a technical discretionary trader, not a systematic one; key lessons are matching style to psychology, optimal bet size with high heat, not tinkering or cutting size in drawdowns, sizing off closed-trade equity.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: if you want to get the optimal return, you have to push that bet size and the heat has to be high and most people can't do it
claims.claim: Seykota's approach shows that maximizing return requires pushing bet size and tolerating large heat, but overshooting the optimum risks ruin, so extreme sizing is not advisable for most traders.
claims.conditions: traders who can psychologically bear very large drawdowns
claims.testable: partly: growth-optimal sizing is analytic but heat tolerance is personal

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: Ed is a technical discretionary trader he wrote all these programs to support the data presentation uh that he then used to make discretionary calls about buying and selling
claims.claim: Seykota is a technical discretionary trader who used custom software only to display charts; the Market Wizards impression that he was a systematic computerized trader is wrong.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: cut your losses short, let your profits ride, diversify
claims.claim: Seykota followed a few sacrosanct general rules: cut losses short, let profits ride, diversify.
claims.testable: partly: rules are testable as stops and trend riding

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: his um his equity swings can be gigantic
claims.claim: Seykota's equity swings are enormous, so no institution would invest in him despite the very high returns, since his aim was maximum profit rather than controlled risk.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: it talks about a jade master
claims.claim: Seykota's teaching is by apprenticeship and observation (the Jade master story in The Trader's Window) rather than explicit rules, so his skill cannot be programmed or taught directly.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: everybody gets what they want from the markets and it's and markets are a a vehicle for people to work out their psychology
claims.claim: In Seykota's view markets expose hidden psychological problems, so unresolved psychology is brought into trading and causes self-sabotage; hence he held group sessions to surface problems.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: at the end of the day when markets closed, we look at charts and it would take about maybe 10 minutes
claims.claim: Seykota spent little time on markets, looking at end-of-day charts for about 10 minutes, deciding approximate entries and stops for next day.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: if your style of trading doesn't fit your psychology you're going to fail
claims.claim: A trading style must match the trader's psychology, since people who cannot follow a computerized system will tinker with it even if it is excellent.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: never listen to the news. What does the chart tell you? What does the price tell you?
claims.claim: Seykota believed technical discretionary trading on price only (ignoring news) earns more than systematic trading.
claims.testable: partly: discretionary chart reading is hard to test

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: you always have to trade with money that's meaningful in order for you to learn and understand yourself
claims.claim: Trading with meaningful size is necessary to learn about oneself, because small money creates no real emotional stakes.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: So, I did this for about 15 months. made 300% return and absolutely went crazy because it was not my trading style
claims.claim: Drew traded a personal account discretionary Seykota-style for 15 months, made 300% while his systems made 20% for investors, yet had to quit and see a psychiatrist because it did not fit him.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: There is actually an optimal bet size if you have a system with a known edge per trade
claims.claim: There is an optimal bet size given a known edge per trade (Seykota and Drew wrote an article on heat distribution), but because edge is unstable over time it is only a rule of thumb, and the optimal size is bigger than most people would use.
claims.testable: yes: simulate growth vs bet size by backtest

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: you go too far and your risk of ruin is douche
claims.claim: Betting too large raises risk of ruin steeply, while betting too little makes risk of ruin near zero but gives low returns.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: you want to make a lot of money you have to bet bigger than you think but not too big
claims.claim: To make a lot of money one must bet bigger than seems comfortable, taking considerable heat, but not so big as to risk ruin.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: every day was new and every day was do the right thing
claims.claim: Seykota showed no memory of recent losses and acted correctly each day, a discipline needed whether discretionary or systematic.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: that's the worst time to change something is in a draw down
claims.claim: The worst time to change a system is during a drawdown; tinkering driven by drawdown psychology harms long-run results, so let statistics play out unless sure something is broken.
claims.testable: partly: compare changes made in drawdown vs not

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: You can't have a draw down reduction rule where you're all of a sudden you know dialing back
claims.claim: Drawdown reduction rules (dialing risk back after losses) can keep a system underwater indefinitely, so size should instead scale with current equity.
claims.direction: do not cut risk beyond equity scaling

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: your bet size needs to change with your equity at some point
claims.claim: Bet size should scale proportionally with equity (2x at 2 million), rising and falling, otherwise risk of ruin rises if you only scale up.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: Open equity it never works really. People can try it but closed equity or or equity after everything got wouldn't be stopped out
claims.claim: Sizing from closed-trade equity (after stops) is more stable than from open-trade equity, which includes large open profits and encourages over-risking.
claims.testable: yes: compare sizing bases in backtest

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: it probably shouldn't be 250,000 which would be too little risk put on to get out of the draw down
claims.claim: After a 50% drawdown bet size should be on the reduced equity base but not cut further, as extra de-risking gives too little risk to recover and distorts the statistics of the system.

claims.speaker: Dave Drew
claims.quote: we limit ourselves in our success in the markets because we don't believe that we are deserving of great success
claims.claim: Seykota held that self-limiting beliefs (not feeling worthy) hold traders back, so psychological clearing is part of success.
